units.title: Unit 55 — Email and the Internet
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 55. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Use key verbs and expressions for sending, receiving, managing and replying to email.
Explain Internet connections, service providers, browsers, links and online access.
Describe Internet searching, downloads, uploads, online shopping and payments.
Distinguish blogs, social networking sites, online comments and instant messaging.
Recognise common email collocations and pronounce email-address components.

items.pt: verificar seus e-mails; conferir a caixa de entrada
items.example: I check my email twice each morning.
items.note: Look to see whether you have received new messages.

items.example: Could you send an email confirming the new date?
items.note: You send a message to another person's email address.

items.example: We received an email with the booking details.
items.note: Receive is more formal than get when describing an incoming message.

items.example: I got an email from the hotel this morning.
items.note: Informal alternative to receive an email.

items.example: A clear subject line is essential in a business email.
items.note: Very important or necessary; not merely convenient.

items.example: Please contact me immediately if the booking changes.
items.note: Without waiting; more emphatic than soon.

items.example: I replied to the email before the meeting.
items.note: Reply to a message or a person; use the preposition to.

items.example: I haven't had a reply to my question yet.
items.note: Verb or noun; a reply is an answer to a message or request.

items.example: Delete that message if it was sent by mistake.
items.note: Remove a message from the mailbox.

items.example: She regularly clears old messages from her inbox.
items.note: Happening repeatedly or at regular intervals.

items.example: My spam folder contains dozens of unwanted emails.
items.note: Unwanted email, often advertising; usually uncountable.

items.example: The filter moves junk mail to a separate folder.
items.note: Another term for unwanted advertising email.

items.example: The email contained an advert for a new service.
items.note: Common British English short form of advertisement.

items.example: Good anti-virus software can help protect your computer.
items.note: Software is uncountable; this term also appears in Unit 54.

items.example: I forgot to include the attachment in my email.
items.note: A file sent together with an email message.

items.example: Could you send the report as an attachment?
items.note: Send a document or other file together with a message.

items.example: Please write your email address on the registration form.
items.note: An address for receiving digital messages, often containing @.

items.pt: arroba (na leitura de endereços de e-mail)
items.example: When reading the address aloud, say at for the @ sign.
items.note: When spoken as part of an email address, @ is pronounced at.

items.pt: ponto (na leitura de endereços da internet)
items.example: Say dot when you read the website address aloud.
items.note: When spelling an email address or domain name, say dot for a full stop.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: Our ISP has improved the connection speed.
items.note: The abbreviation stands for Internet service provider.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: We changed our Internet service provider last month.
items.note: A company that connects people or organisations to the Internet.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: The hotel allows guests to connect to the Internet.
items.note: Connect to something; to is required here.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: The Internet connection stopped during the call.
items.note: The noun related to connect; a connection may be fast, slow or unreliable.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: There is free access to the Internet in the library.
items.note: Access to a service means the ability or right to use it.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: Internet access is included in the room price.
items.note: Common noun phrase; access is normally uncountable in this sense.

items.pt: dar acesso a algo para alguém
items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: The school gives students access to its online library.
items.note: The structure is give someone access to something.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: The timetable is available online.
items.note: Adverb or adjective for activities or services on the Internet.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: I usually go online to compare train prices.
items.note: Start using or connect to the Internet.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: We browsed the Internet for travel ideas.
items.note: Look through websites, not necessarily with a particular destination.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: You can open the webpage in any modern browser.
items.note: Software used for visiting and viewing websites.

items.pt: site; página ou conjunto de páginas da internet
items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: The museum's website lists admission prices.
items.note: A collection of webpages with an Internet address.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: The link in the message takes you to the timetable.
items.note: A clickable connection to another page or part of a website.

items.section: B · Getting started on the Internet
items.example: Click on the link to view the instructions.
items.note: Click on something; the preposition on is part of the book's expression.

items.example: I searched the Internet for instructions on the new software.
items.note: Look online for information; often followed by for plus the topic.

items.example: Do an Internet search before choosing a hotel.
items.note: A noun-phrase alternative to search the Internet.

items.example: You can download the timetable as a PDF.
items.note: Verb: copy data from an Internet service onto your device; compare upload.

items.example: Upload your photograph before submitting the form.
items.note: Verb: send a file from your device to a website or service; opposite of download.

items.pt: clipe de vídeo; trecho curto de vídeo
items.example: She shared a short video clip from the concert.
items.note: A brief part of a video recording.

items.example: It's easy to buy tickets online.
items.note: Pay for a product or service through the Internet.

items.pt: reservar férias ou viagem pela internet
items.example: We booked our holiday online last week.
items.note: Book means arrange and reserve, not read a book.

items.example: We took out travel insurance before flying.
items.note: Take out insurance means arrange to buy an insurance policy.

items.example: Select an item and check the delivery options.
items.note: Select means choose; item means a particular product in online shopping.

items.example: That item is not currently available.
items.note: A single thing or product, especially on a shopping website.

items.example: Click Add to basket to save the product for checkout.
items.note: Common British online-shopping command; bag or cart may be used on other websites.

items.pt: ir para a etapa de finalizar a compra
items.example: Go to checkout when you have chosen everything.
items.note: At checkout you confirm the order and pay.

items.example: Check the delivery address at checkout.
items.note: The shopping stage where an order is completed; distinct from the verb check out.

items.example: You can pay by credit card on this website.
items.note: A natural method-of-payment phrase; a card is used to pay for items.

items.example: She used a credit card to pay for the order.
items.note: A card used to borrow money for purchases until repayment.

items.example: His personal website includes a travel diary.
items.note: A website mainly about a person or their interests.

items.example: I follow a blog about learning languages.
items.note: A website with posts about a topic or somebody's experiences.

items.example: The blogger writes about local restaurants.
items.note: A person who writes and publishes a blog.

items.example: He sometimes surfs the web after dinner.
items.note: Informal expression for visiting many websites without a specific task.

items.example: Many people share photos on social networking sites.
items.note: A website where people connect and interact with others.

items.example: Visitors can post a comment below the article.
items.note: Post means publish a message where others can see it.

items.pt: mensagens instantâneas; troca de mensagens em tempo real
items.example: We use instant messaging to arrange team meetings.
items.note: Sending and receiving short messages almost immediately.

items.example: Students send and receive messages through the app.
items.note: Common paired communication verbs: send is outgoing and receive is incoming.

sectionsChecked: A: Using email, message management, unwanted mail, attachments and spoken email addresses
B: Getting started on the Internet, ISP, online access, browsers and links
C: Using the Internet, searches, file transfer, online shopping, blogs and social communication
Exercises 55.1–55.4 and Unit 55 answer key, including Internet collocations and email vocabulary

units.title: Unit 56 — Crime
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 56. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish crime, theft, robbery, burglary and murder and their corresponding people and verbs.
Use accurate verb-object patterns for steal, rob and burgle.
Understand media reports of break-ins, attacks, arrests and escapes.
Describe offences, investigation, court proceedings, verdicts and punishments.
Recognise important semantic oppositions including guilty/innocent and minor/serious.

items.example: The police reported a rise in crime in the area.
items.note: An act that is against the law; crime can refer to one act or to crime in general.

items.example: He was arrested after committing a serious crime.
items.note: Commit is the usual verb with a crime; not make a crime.

items.example: The police are still searching for the criminal.
items.note: A person who commits a crime; also an adjective, as in criminal activity.

items.example: The museum reported the theft of a valuable painting.
items.note: The act of stealing; the source contrasts theft with robbery and burglary.

items.example: A thief took her phone from her bag.
items.note: Person noun for someone who steals; plural thieves.

items.example: Someone tried to steal my bicycle.
items.note: Steal something from someone or a place; steal-stole-stolen.

items.example: A thief stole two wallets during the concert.
items.note: Past simple form of steal.

items.example: The police recovered the stolen jewellery.
items.note: Past participle of steal; often used as an adjective.

items.example: The bank closed early after a robbery.
items.note: Stealing from a person or place, often by threat or force; noun related to rob.

items.example: A robber demanded money from the shop assistant.
items.note: A person who robs a person or place.

items.example: Two men tried to rob a tourist near the station.
items.note: Rob somebody, a shop or a bank; steal an object. Do not say rob a wallet.

items.example: Nobody was hurt during the bank robbery.
items.note: A robbery at a bank; a common crime-related collocation.

items.pt: arrombamento e furto em imóvel; invasão de imóvel para furtar
items.example: The neighbours reported a burglary while the family was away.
items.note: Entering a building illegally, typically to steal; distinct from robbery.

items.example: The burglar entered the house through a window.
items.note: A person who enters a building illegally to steal.

items.pt: invadir uma casa para furtar; cometer furto em residência
items.example: Someone burgled a house at the end of our street.
items.note: British English: burgle a building, rather than burgle an item.

items.example: The detectives are investigating a murder.
items.note: Noun or verb for the unlawful intentional killing of another person.

items.pt: assassino; autora ou autor de homicídio
items.example: The murderer was found guilty in court.
items.note: Person noun derived from murder.

items.example: The man was accused of murdering his neighbour.
items.note: Use murder as a transitive verb with a person as its object.

items.pt: invadir um local à força; arrombar para entrar
items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: Thieves broke in during the night.
items.note: Intransitive phrasal verb for illegally entering a building; past broke in.

items.pt: invadir um prédio; entrar por arrombamento
items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: The thieves broke into a building near the market.
items.note: Break into is transitive and takes the place entered as its object.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: The stolen watches were worth several thousand pounds.
items.note: Used with a value: worth £500, worth a lot of money.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: Two men attacked the driver and ran away.
items.note: Verb and noun for using violence against someone or something.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: The attacker hit him in the arm.
items.note: Verb for striking someone; hit-hit-hit.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: The suspect escaped through an open window.
items.note: Leave a place or situation to avoid being caught or harmed.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: The thief got away before the police arrived.
items.note: Phrasal verb meaning escape; past got away.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: A detective spoke to the witnesses.
items.note: A police officer who investigates crimes.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: Officers arrested the suspect outside the station.
items.note: Verb or noun: police take someone into custody because they suspect a crime.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: The officer told the driver that he was under arrest.
items.note: Fixed phrase describing someone formally arrested.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: A police officer asked us to remain calm.
items.note: One member of the police service.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: The suspect was taken to the police station.
items.note: A building where police officers work and people may be held or questioned.

items.section: B · Reporting crimes in the media
items.example: Officers caught the criminal near the bus stop.
items.note: Catch means find and stop someone trying to avoid arrest.

items.example: The judge considered the appropriate punishment.
items.note: The penalty or consequence for doing something wrong.

items.example: The court will punish people who break the law.
items.note: Verb related to punishment.

items.example: Driving without a valid licence is an offence.
items.note: British spelling of offense; an act against the law or rules.

items.pt: infração leve; delito de menor gravidade
items.example: He received a small fine for a minor offence.
items.note: A less serious violation; opposite in this context is serious offence.

items.example: The report described a serious crime in the city centre.
items.note: A crime with grave consequences, contrasted with a minor offence.

items.example: She had to pay a fine for the parking offence.
items.note: Noun for a monetary penalty; fine can also be a verb.

items.example: He paid a fine instead of going to court.
items.note: Use pay with the noun fine.

items.pt: ir ao tribunal; comparecer à Justiça
items.example: The case may go to court next month.
items.note: Be dealt with by a court of law; no article in this fixed expression.

items.example: Several witnesses were questioned in court.
items.note: The place or institution where legal cases are decided.

items.example: The judge explained the decision to the jury.
items.note: A person who controls legal proceedings and gives judgments.

items.example: The jury listened carefully to the evidence.
items.note: A group of citizens deciding facts or guilt in some trials.

items.example: The court found him guilty of theft.
items.note: Someone is guilty of a crime if they committed it; opposite innocent.

items.example: She was found innocent after the trial.
items.note: Not guilty of the alleged wrongdoing; opposite of guilty.

items.pt: considerado culpado; condenado por decisão judicial
items.example: The defendant was found guilty of robbery.
items.note: Legal pattern: be found guilty of a crime.

items.example: The court found her innocent of the accusation.
items.note: The book uses found innocent; in many legal contexts found not guilty is more usual.

items.example: The man was sent to prison after the trial.
items.note: A place where people are held as punishment or before trial.

items.example: He spent several months in jail.
items.note: Common synonym for prison; meanings and usage vary by country.

items.pt: ser preso; ir para a prisão
items.example: If convicted, he could go to prison.
items.note: Fixed expression meaning be imprisoned; no article in this usage.

items.pt: condenar alguém à prisão; enviar alguém para a prisão
items.example: The judge sent the offender to prison.
items.note: A court may send a convicted person to prison.

items.pt: violar a lei; infringir a lei
items.example: People who break the law may face penalties.
items.note: Common expression meaning act illegally.

items.example: The company keeps spare parts in a warehouse.
items.note: A large building used to store goods, explained in the practice news report.

items.example: Police charged the suspect with robbery.
items.note: Charge someone with a crime is a formal legal accusation.

sectionsChecked: A: Different crimes; noun-person-verb chart and examples distinguishing theft, robbery, burglary and murder
B: Reporting crimes in the media; break in, worth, attack, escape, detectives and arrest
C: Punishment; minor and serious offences, fines, court, verdicts, prison and jury
Exercises 56.1–56.4 and Unit 56 answer key, including law, warehouse and charges in the news report
